messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Karim is a 41-year-old construction worker who grew up in a home where his father’s rages shaped the atmosphere of daily life. The memory that stays with him most comes from when he was a boy hiding near the kitchen doorway while his father cornered his mother during an argument, shouting in Arabic and English, knocking a chair aside, and raising his hand as she tried to make herself smaller. Certain parts are burned into him with unnatural sharpness: the shine of the overhead light on the linoleum, his mother’s bracelet twisted against her wrist, the exact angle of his father’s face when he turned toward the noise Karim made. Other parts are missing altogether. He says it is like looking at scattered photographs rather than remembering a whole scene, and when he tries on purpose to fill in what happened before or after those images, his mind goes blank.

That fragmented way of remembering has made the present feel treacherously connected to the past. On job sites, confrontations between foremen and workers can pull those images up without warning, especially when voices harden or a man steps into someone else’s space. Seeing police near a work zone or being approached by any uniformed authority brings the same jolt, as if danger has already arrived before anything has happened. Even conversations that should be ordinary, like coworkers asking where he sees himself in five years, catch him off guard; talking about the future feels unreal and exposed, and he finds himself pulled back toward old scenes instead of forward into plans. The more the memory comes in flashes he cannot fully control or deliberately sort through, the more these situations become charged and easier to set off.

When Karim is triggered, his body reacts first. He feels heat climb up his neck, his chest tighten, and his stomach drop. He watches faces closely, scanning for the first sign that irritation is turning into threat, and if a supervisor pauses too long before answering a question or a text from a family member goes unanswered, he quickly assumes something bad is happening. Those reactions make sense to him; he has come to believe that trouble announces itself in expressions, posture, and ominous silences, and that missing those signs would be dangerous. In those moments, the old memory seems even more vivid in fragments, with one frozen image suddenly dominating his mind while the rest stays inaccessible.

Over the years he has developed ways of getting through that often narrow his life. At work he avoids any situation that might involve disagreement. If there is confusion about assignments or unfair criticism, he is more likely to back away, keep his head down, or switch tasks than risk a confrontation. When conversations turn toward promotions, relationships, or long-term plans, he drifts off into a private fantasy world or starts dwelling on how different he was before all of this took hold, when he imagines he was less vigilant and more open. These habits are strongest after he has been set off by an argument, an authority figure, or talk about the future, and they have cost him; supervisors see him as hard to read and sometimes disengaged, and he has passed up chances for steadier roles because he cannot tolerate the scrutiny that comes with them.

Those strategies, however, seem to keep the problem alive. Avoiding conflict leaves him with fewer chances to learn that raised voices do not always end in violence, and drifting away mentally during tense moments makes the present blur while isolated images from childhood remain painfully crisp. Dwelling on who he used to be pulls him back toward the past and makes any future-oriented conversation feel even more loaded. He notices that the more he escapes into his head or backs away from disagreement, the more he studies people for danger afterward and the more easily delays or stern expressions trigger him. At times, after zoning out during a tense exchange, he is left again with that same patchwork quality in memory: one clear snapshot, missing stretches around it, and frustration when he tries deliberately to make coherent sense of it.

His threat monitoring also feeds that pattern. Because he is constantly reading faces and bracing for the worst in moments of uncertainty, his attention locks onto details that resemble the original scenes of violence. He can describe a foreman’s clenched jaw or a police officer’s stance with photographic precision, while the broader context slips away. That selective intensity makes the world feel full of reminders and confirms his sense that he has to keep avoiding, withdrawing, and disappearing into fantasy to stay steady.

Karim finally sought help after an incident on a construction site when two men began arguing near a police detail assigned to street work. He felt his body surge, lost track of the conversation around him, and spent the rest of the shift detached and shaky, unable to remember parts of what had been said to him. What frightened him most was not just the reaction itself, but the sense that his life has become organized around anticipating danger and retreating from it. He says he wants “to be here when things happen instead of somewhere else,” and he is afraid that if nothing changes, he will remain trapped between frozen pictures of the past and a future he cannot bear to imagine.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that the traumatic memory itself causes or increases triggers/reminders, rather than triggers bringing up the memory.
The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Karim’s sense of threat directly leads to the trauma memory becoming activated or more intrusive.
